title: Firecrawl vs. Browserbase vs. Bright Data for AI Agents
summary: Firecrawl vs Browserbase vs Bright Data for AI agents: per-page vs browser-hour vs per-GB pricing, what each does in 2026,…
body_markdown:
Pick by what your agent has to do on the page. Firecrawl fits per-page extraction into markdown or JSON, Browserbase fits long, stateful browser sessions billed by the browser hour, and Bright Data fits high-volume collection where IP diversity decides whether requests get through. The lines have blurred in 2026: Firecrawl now has an Interact endpoint for clicks and logins, Browserbase sells a stateless Fetch API, and Bright Data prices its Web Unlocker per successful request. Anakin covers the common middle ground from one API key: HTTP scraping by default, a browser when a page needs one, and a cloud browser or a Wire action when the agent has to log in. Below, we compare the three architectures, what each one costs at 10,000 tasks, and when each is worth it.


## Key takeaways


- Firecrawl is built around per-page API scraping into markdown or JSON, and its newer Interact endpoint adds clicks, form fills and saved login profiles, billed per browser minute
- Browserbase provides cloud browser sessions that keep cookies and login state across multi-step workflows, billed by the browser hour
- Bright Data runs a 400M+ residential IP network across 195 countries for high-volume collection where IP rotation decides success
- Session-aware fallback architectures start with HTTP scraping and escalate to browser rendering only when needed
- Cost models differ: credits per page (Firecrawl), browser hours (Browserbase), gigabytes or successful requests (Bright Data), credits per successful job (Anakin)


## How AI agents access web data: three architectural patterns


An agent can reach web data in three ways. Stateless API extraction, the Firecrawl model, sends a URL and gets clean content back with no session state between calls. Persistent cloud browsers, the Browserbase model, keep cookies and login state across steps and bill for the time the browser stays open. Proxy-mediated requests, the Bright Data model, route traffic through residential IPs so it looks like ordinary users, which matters most where IP reputation is the main signal. Each solves a different problem, and the table maps them side by side before the sections below go through each tool.


Tool Best for Session handling Primary output Billing model


Firecrawl Single-task HTTP extraction Stateless by default; Interact adds logged-in steps Markdown Per-page credit


Browserbase Multi-step interactive workflows Persistent browser sessions DOM snapshots Per browser hour


Bright Data Large-scale anti-bot evasion Stateless with proxy rotation Raw HTML / datasets Per GB (proxies) or per successful request (Web Unlocker)


Anakin HTTP-first with browser escalation HTTP-first, browser mode when needed Markdown / JSON Credits per successful job


Values are editorial assessments based on available documentation, not independently benchmarked figures.


## Firecrawl: API-first scraping for structured extraction


Firecrawl is an extraction API optimized for AI workflows. You submit a URL; it returns markdown or structured JSON. The platform handles JavaScript rendering, anti-bot measures, and content cleaning, all behind a single REST call, and it reports a[P95 latency of 3.4 seconds](https://www.firecrawl.dev/) on its own 1,000-URL benchmark. Firecrawl positions itself as delivering "AI-ready data" rather than raw HTML, addressing the gap between traditional scrapers and the specific formats generative AI systems require.


### How Firecrawl processes web pages for AI agents


A single scrape call returns its result directly, while crawls and batch scrapes run as async jobs that hand back a job ID to poll. Each scrape request is stateless unless you attach Interact or a saved profile. The API returns markdown for LLM consumption or structured JSON when you specify an extraction schema. This design fits batch workflows where an agent submits many URLs, polls in parallel, and aggregates results.


### Cost structure and developer experience


Firecrawl bills per page, a flat model where a page that takes 10 seconds to render costs the same as one that loads in 500ms. The free tier gives 1,000 credits a month, and[paid plans](https://www.firecrawl.dev/pricing) run from $16/month (5,000 credits) to $333/month (500,000 credits), billed annually, as listed on 25 Oct 2026. Python and Node SDKs hide the polling loop. The trade-off has moved: Firecrawl's[Interact endpoint](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/interact) can now click, fill forms and reuse a saved login profile, but it bills per browser minute (2 credits a minute, 7 when driven by a prompt), so long multi-step flows land on the same time-based meter as a cloud browser.


### Best use cases for AI agents


Choose Firecrawl when your agent mostly does stateless extraction: scraping product listings, aggregating news articles, pulling documentation pages. The markdown output plugs into LangChain, AutoGen and other agent frameworks without extra parsing. The flat per-page model stays cost-efficient for hundreds or thousands of pages a month that don't need a persistent browser. When volume reaches tens of thousands of pages monthly, compare the per-page cost against the time-based or bandwidth-based models of Browserbase and Bright Data. Anakin's[URL Scraper](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/url-scraper/submit-scrape-job) covers the same job, with proxy routing across 207 countries, async jobs you poll or receive by webhook and optional AI JSON extraction, at 1 credit per page, doesn't charge for failed jobs, and serves repeat requests from cache up to 30x faster.


For agents whose whole job is a long authenticated session, a per-page API with browser add-ons gets awkward. A dedicated cloud browser is the more natural fit.


## Browserbase: managed browser infrastructure for persistent sessions


Browserbase handles production AI agent workloads through persistent browser sessions that keep cookies, login state and JavaScript context across multi-step workflows. It reported 1,000+ customers when it raised a[$40M Series B](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/browserbase-launches-director-to-automate-the-web-for-everyone-announces-40m-series-b-302483761.html) in June 2025, and its homepage now cites 10,000+ companies. Its pitch to developers rests on session replay and Stagehand, its own automation framework.


### Session lifecycle management for multi-step workflows


Browserbase keeps browser contexts alive so agents log in once, run a sequence of interactions, and keep login state across API calls. Sessions last for the duration of the workflow (up to 15 minutes per session on the free plan), which is what scraping login-gated content or driving JavaScript-heavy single-page apps requires. That persistence has a cost: a live browser consumes compute whether the agent is acting or idle. For workflows that don't need state, stateless scraping responds faster and costs less per request.


### When browser state matters vs. when it's overhead


Browser sessions are necessary when agents work with login-protected content, submit multi-step forms, or scrape JavaScript-rendered SPAs where content doesn't exist in the initial HTML. For these cases, persistent state is non-negotiable. For static pages or API-accessible data, a browser adds latency and cost with no functional benefit. Session-based workflows pay browser startup time and browser-hour billing, while stateless scraping returns results faster and bills per successful request.


### Pricing model and latency considerations


Browserbase[bills by the browser hour](https://www.browserbase.com/pricing) : the $20 Developer plan includes 100 hours, then $0.12 an hour, and the $99 Startup plan includes 500 hours, then $0.10 (listed on 25 Oct 2026). A 10,000-task workflow where each session runs 3 minutes adds up to 500 browser hours, the full Startup allowance. Cost tracks session duration, not result count. Browser startup also adds latency that an HTTP-only call never pays. For pages that don't need a session, Browserbase now sells a stateless Fetch API at $1 per 1,000 calls on the Developer plan. Anakin's[Browser API](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/browser-api) works the same way: agents connect Playwright or Puppeteer over a single WebSocket URL and save a login with` save_session` . The same 10,000 three-minute sessions would cost 20,000 credits there, since each session is billed in 2-minute windows. Model cost at your real volume: stateless APIs bill per successful extraction; session-based platforms bill for the time the browser stays provisioned.


When browser rendering alone cannot evade aggressive rate limiting or IP blacklists, enterprise proxy networks provide the infrastructure layer needed for large-scale anti-bot bypass.


## Bright Data: enterprise proxy networks for anti-bot bypass


### Proxy architecture and anti-bot mechanisms


Bright Data's[residential network](https://brightdata.com/proxy-types/residential-proxies) lists 400M+ IPs in 195 countries, and its unblocking products handle CAPTCHAs. Rotation happens on Bright Data's side, and agents can target a country, state, city or ZIP code without maintaining their own IP pool. Residential rotation spreads requests across many real-device endpoints, so traffic looks like ordinary users rather than a data center. That helps most where IP reputation is the main signal; systems such as Cloudflare and DataDome also check browser fingerprints, so proxies alone don't clear every challenge.


### Cost structure: bandwidth vs. request pricing


Bright Data's residential proxies bill by the gigabyte, not per request or per browser hour. For AI agents running 10,000 tasks a day, monthly cost depends on average payload size, a variable that per-page (Firecrawl) and per-hour (Browserbase) pricing don't have. A typical HTML scrape uses 50 to 200 KB, while JS-rendered pages with images can reach 2 to 5 MB. At 10K tasks × 500 KB average × 30 days = 150 GB/month. At the[pay-as-you-go list price](https://brightdata.com/pricing/proxy-network/residential-proxies) of $8/GB shown on 25 Oct 2026, that is about $1,200 a month (about $600 at the 50% promotional rate running that day), and committed plans start at $499 a month for 141 GB. Teams that prefer per-request pricing can use Bright Data's[Web Unlocker](https://brightdata.com/pricing/web-unlocker) , which starts at $1 per 1,000 requests and charges only for successful ones.


### Enterprise scale and integration complexity


Bright Data fits AI deployments where unblocking success justifies the integration work. Raw proxy use means configuring endpoint URLs and authentication, handling retries, and watching bandwidth, which takes more setup than an API-only scraping service. Bright Data's network is built for heavily protected sites, but teams on raw proxies debug failures at the network layer rather than behind an abstracted scraping API. Best for: enterprise data operations running 10K+ requests a day against sites with known anti-bot defenses, and teams with the engineering capacity to instrument proxy routing and monitor bandwidth in real time. Teams that want geo-routing without running a proxy layer can pass a` country` parameter to Anakin's URL Scraper, which covers[207 countries and territories](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/supported-countries) behind one API call.


Rather than committing to a single pattern upfront, hybrid approaches automatically select the right infrastructure based on target complexity, starting with fast HTTP requests and escalating only when necessary.


## Anakin: unified scraping with automatic browser escalation


[Anakin](https://anakin.io/) combines the API-first simplicity of Firecrawl with the browser-rendering capability of Browserbase through automatic escalation. Agents get the speed of HTTP scraping with a fallback to browser mode when needed, without managing two separate tools.


### How session-aware fallback works


Anakin URL Scraper starts with standard HTTP scraping, the fastest and cheapest path for most targets. For SPAs and dynamically loaded pages, agents add` useBrowser: true` to trigger headless Chrome rendering. The system handles JavaScript rendering, proxy routing, retries, anti-bot handling and authenticated browser sessions under the hood. When anti-bot responses are detected (403, CAPTCHA, JavaScript challenges), it escalates to browser rendering automatically, so agents don't have to choose upfront.


### Cost and performance trade-offs


Hybrid pricing means agents pay for browser mode only when they need it: cheaper than always-on browser sessions, with some added latency during escalation. Anakin's async job pattern separates submission from retrieval, so agents submit tasks, poll for results, and never block the pipeline. This model saves money on mixed workloads (simple pages plus protected targets) but adds overhead if every request needs browser rendering. In that case, a dedicated browser such as Anakin's Browser API or Browserbase, or a proxy network such as Bright Data, may fit better.


### Integration with AI agent frameworks


Anakin has documented integrations for[LangChain](https://anakin.io/docs/integrations/ai-frameworks/langchain) , CrewAI and[Dify](https://anakin.io/docs/integrations/workflow/dify) , plus an MCP server for agent clients. Agents submit URLs to a single endpoint, control JavaScript rendering and proxy location through API parameters, and never manage headless browsers directly. Choose Anakin when agents need HTTP scraping for speed plus browser fallback for protected pages without two separate tools. For workflows that always need a browser (visual testing, long client-side interactions), a dedicated browser is simpler. For proxy-heavy collection at very high volume, Bright Data's 400M+ IP network is built for the job.


## So which one should your agent use?


Firecrawl is the quickest path from URL to markdown or JSON, and its Interact endpoint now covers short logged-in steps at browser-minute rates. Browserbase gives full browser state for long, stateful workflows, billed by the browser hour. Bright Data's residential network is the specialist choice when IP diversity decides whether requests get through, billed per GB or per successful request.


### Use case 1: single-task data extraction


**Choose Firecrawl when:** Your agent performs isolated scraping tasks without session state: fetching product listings, extracting article content, or converting pages to markdown for RAG pipelines. Firecrawl bills per page scraped, so costs stay predictable when job volume is stable. Because it handles JavaScript rendering and anti-bot measures behind a single endpoint, agents can issue HTTP requests without managing headless browsers. For logins, search submission or multi-step navigation, Firecrawl's Interact endpoint works, but billing moves to browser minutes, so compare it against a dedicated browser at that point.


### Use case 2: multi-step interactive workflows


**Choose Browserbase when:** Your agent needs persistent browser sessions for login or navigation: signing into a SaaS dashboard, clicking through paginated results, or filling forms across multiple pages. Browserbase runs a stateful browser that agents control via CDP or Playwright, keeping cookies and session tokens between steps. This is the right infrastructure when the workflow itself is the product, not just the data extracted. **Choose Anakin when:** The site blocks simple HTTP but doesn't require persistent login. Anakin's URL Scraper lets agents start with standard HTTP and switch to browser mode with` useBrowser: true` for JavaScript-heavy pages, and its` actions` parameter can click, scroll or wait before the page is captured (+1 credit). When the agent does need a login, Anakin's[saved browser sessions](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/browser-api/saved-sessions) or a pre-built[Wire](https://anakin.io/products/wire) action on one of 973 supported sites (as of 25 Oct 2026) keep the work on the same API key.


### Use case 3: large-scale anti-bot evasion


**Choose Bright Data when:** Your agent faces aggressive bot detection at high request volumes: scraping e-commerce catalogs, monitoring competitor pricing, or collecting SERP data at scale. Bright Data's 400M+ IP proxy network is purpose-built for that kind of unblocking. Its Web Unlocker bills per successful request, so failed requests cost nothing, while raw residential proxies bill per GB. This is the path to take when sites run sophisticated fingerprinting and your agent must spread requests across residential IPs to avoid rate limits. Before signing a proxy contract, it is worth testing protected targets on Anakin's URL Scraper, where failed jobs aren't charged either.


For workflows that combine stateless extraction with occasional browser-mode needs,[Anakin's infrastructure guide](https://anakin.io/blog/infra-continuously-updating-ai-systems-web-data) explains how async job orchestration decouples submission from retrieval, letting agents batch multiple URLs without blocking on per-request latency.


For most AI agent teams, the deciding question is the one this comparison opened with: what does the agent have to do on the page? Most workloads mix plain pages, JavaScript-heavy pages and the occasional login, and that mix is where one API beats two integrations. Anakin's URL Scraper covers proxy routing across 207 countries, async jobs and browser mode via` useBrowser: true` , and the Browser API and Wire cover logged-in work on the same key. Start there, then add Browserbase or Bright Data when a workload outgrows it.


Start with[Anakin's free tier](https://anakin.io/) (300 credits, no card required) to test HTTP extraction and browser escalation on your AI agent workflows, then scale to dedicated browser infrastructure (Browserbase) or enterprise proxies (Bright Data) only when your use case demands it.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### When should an AI agent use Firecrawl vs Browserbase?


Use Firecrawl when your agent mostly extracts pages without logging in: product listings, news articles, documentation. Its Interact endpoint can handle short logged-in steps at browser-minute rates. Choose Browserbase when the browser session is the workflow itself: long login-protected sessions, multi-step form submissions, or JavaScript-rendered SPAs where session state is non-negotiable.


### How much does it cost to run 10,000 AI agent scraping tasks per month?


It depends on each vendor's billing unit. Firecrawl charges 1 credit per basic page, so 10,000 pages fit in its Standard plan's 100,000 monthly credits ($99/month, or $83 billed annually). Browserbase bills browser hours: 10,000 three-minute sessions add up to 500 hours, the allowance in its $99 Startup plan. Bright Data residential proxies bill per GB, so cost = tasks × average payload size × price per GB; at 500 KB a page, 10,000 pages is about 5 GB. On Anakin, 10,000 basic page scrapes cost 10,000 credits, and failed jobs aren't charged. Prices as listed on 25 Oct 2026.


### What is session-aware fallback and why does it matter for AI agents?


Session-aware fallback starts with fast HTTP scraping and automatically escalates to headless browser rendering when anti-bot measures are detected. This architecture lets agents avoid paying for browser infrastructure on every request while still handling JavaScript-heavy sites and SPAs when needed, combining cost efficiency with reliability without upfront infrastructure commitment.


### Can Bright Data's proxies be used with Firecrawl or Browserbase?


Bright Data's proxies work with any client that accepts a proxy setting. Browserbase supports custom proxies on its Developer plan and above, so you can route its sessions through Bright Data residential IPs. Hosted scraping APIs such as Firecrawl run their own proxy layer, so check their docs before assuming you can bring your own. Either way, you pay for both services.


### Do these tools integrate with Langchain or Autogen agent frameworks?


Firecrawl provides official Python and Node SDKs that work with LangChain and AutoGen through custom tool classes. Browserbase connects through Playwright, Puppeteer or its Stagehand framework, which takes more setup than a single REST call. Bright Data supplies proxy endpoints that any HTTP client can use, so integration happens at the network layer rather than through framework-specific adapters. Anakin has LangChain and CrewAI integrations and an MCP server.


### When is browser automation overkill for AI agent scraping?


Browser automation is overkill when target sites serve static HTML or simple JavaScript that doesn't require full rendering, when no authentication or session state is needed, and when sites lack aggressive anti-bot measures. In these cases, API-first scraping delivers faster response times and lower costs without the infrastructure overhead of persistent browser sessions.


### How do you choose between residential proxies and browser rendering for anti-bot bypass?


Use residential proxies (Bright Data) when the primary anti-bot mechanism is IP-based, rate limiting, geofencing, or IP blacklists. Use browser rendering (Browserbase) when sites detect headless browsers via JavaScript fingerprinting or require real browser behavior like mouse movements and timing. The most aggressive sites require both patterns together.
